title: Social network transitions among middle-aged Australians: Relationship with health-related quality of life, loneliness, and social isolation.
abstract: This study aims to identify transitions in social network characteristics over time and whether such transitions predict subsequent health-related quality of life, loneliness, and social isolation. We included nationally representative panel data of 3192 Australians aged 45 to 64. Latent transition analysis examined eight social network indicators assessed at 2010 and 2018 to reveal the corresponding transitions between social network profiles. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the relationship between transition profiles with outcomes of interest measured in 2018. We found minimal transitions during the study period: Most participants sustained their interactions (either diverse or relatively restricted), while about 3% of participants expanded and 8% constricted their network. Compared to individuals with sustained restricted profiles across time, those who constricted their networks were more likely to be isolated (Odd Ratio 1.68, 95% Confidence Interval 1.09-3.18), and those who transitioned toward more expansive networks were less likely to be isolated (0.24, 0.03-0.95). Participants who expanded their social interactions were more likely to report good mental health status compared to participants who maintained restricted social interactions (2.66, 1.16-6.12). Healthy ageing policies should consider supporting diverse community participation and engagement, and quality relationships.
